title: Computable reductions and the undecidability of first-order logic
summary: Translate decision problems by total computable maps, then use the finite Robinson axioms to prove that first-order validity and satisfiability are undecidable.
abstract: Can a program decide whether a sentence is true in every structure interpreting its symbols? A many-one reduction tests the consequences of such a decision procedure by translating inputs with a total computable map that preserves both yes and no answers. Every computably enumerable problem, whose positive instances can be recognized, reduces to the halting problem. A different reduction carries the undecidability of theoremhood in Robinson arithmetic, a finitely axiomatized theory of basic arithmetic, to validity in the fixed language of zero, successor, addition and multiplication. Validity here assumes no arithmetic axioms: the symbols may have arbitrary interpretations. Valid sentences in this language can be recognized by proof search but cannot be decided. Satisfiable sentences, which are true in at least one such structure, cannot even be recognized by a procedure that halts exactly on positive instances.
